articles.title: Agentic AI in one page: agents, tools, memory, MCP and multi-agent patterns
articles.scope: Foundation entry point for the section. Defines agentic AI against generative AI and classic ML, then names the building blocks (tools, memory, MCP, multi-agent communication, workflow orchestration) and typical business uses, each linked to its deep page. Afterwards the reader can answer fundamentals-exam questions on agentic AI.

articles.title: Agents vs agentic workflows vs single LLM calls
articles.scope: Defines an agent as a model that picks its own next action in a loop. Contrasts it with predefined workflows, chatbots, RPA and single calls along an autonomy spectrum, using the AB-100 taxonomy (prompt-and-response, task and autonomous agents; 'retrieval agent' as an alias). States the rule 'if a function will do, don't use an agent'. Afterwards the reader can justify the least-autonomous design that meets a requirement.

articles.title: The agent loop: context, model call, tool execution, stop
articles.scope: Walks one iteration step by step (assemble context, call the model, parse tool calls, execute, append results) and the stop conditions (final answer, iteration budget, timeout, error). Builds a minimal loop with no framework in C# and Python and shows where frameworks and harnesses take over.

articles.title: Agent harness vs framework vs runtime vs platform
articles.scope: Separates four layers: a framework you code against, a harness that runs a ready-made loop, a runtime that hosts and isolates sessions, and a platform that bundles models, tools, identity and governance. A vendor-usage table shows how the word 'harness' differs: a runtime in Copilot Studio, an opinionated agent class in Agent Framework, a managed loop in AgentCore, and a library in the Claude Agent SDK and GitHub Copilot SDK. Afterwards the reader can pick a layer for each concern.

articles.title: ReAct vs plan-and-execute vs reflection
articles.scope: Compares interleaved reason-act-observe loops, upfront planning with re-planning, and self-critique loops, alongside native reasoning models. Notes that Reflexion is one specific published method, not a synonym. Covers cost, latency, error recovery and when chain-of-thought prompting is enough. Implemented in code and in AWS Step Functions.

articles.title: Tool use and function calling
articles.scope: Covers how tools are described (name, description, JSON Schema 2020-12), tool choice, parallel calls, structured outputs, server-side vs client-side tools, argument validation and error handling. Explains why tool descriptions act as prompts. Shows the same tool in the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions, Responses and Bedrock Converse shapes in C# and Python. Also covers (merged from structured-outputs-and-tool-calling): Explains constrained decoding and schema enforcement, contrasting JSON mode, strict structured outputs and tool calling (schemas, tool_choice, parallel calls, round-trips, validation and retry). Compares OpenAI-style tools on Foundry and Bedrock with Converse toolConfig; agent loops go to ai/agents and MCP to ai/protocols.

articles.title: Agent memory: short-term, long-term, episodic, semantic, procedural
articles.scope: Separates session context from persisted memory, and memory from knowledge retrieval (RAG). Covers extraction, consolidation, scoping by user or actor, forgetting and privacy. Maps to AgentCore Memory strategies, Foundry memory (preview), Copilot Studio memory and framework memory providers.

articles.title: Human-in-the-loop vs human-on-the-loop
articles.scope: Covers approval gates, approval-required tools, return of control, interrupts and resume, MCP elicitation, confidence-based escalation and handover to human agents. Shows Agent Framework request/response steps, AgentCore Harness inline function tools, Step Functions callbacks, Amazon A2I review loops, Copilot Studio workflow controls and Customer Conversation harness escalation. Flags the Foundry workflow HITL node as retiring on 2026-12-01.

articles.title: Durable execution for long-running agents
articles.scope: Explains checkpoint and replay, idempotent tool calls, resumable sessions and long waits without paying for compute. Compares LangGraph checkpointers, Agent Framework workflow checkpoints, Foundry hosted-agent background mode, resilient execution and state store (sessions deleted after 30 days idle), AgentCore persistent filesystems and Instances (up to 14 days), the MCP Tasks extension, A2A long-running tasks, Azure Durable Functions, Step Functions and Lambda durable functions. Links messaging/delivery-semantics and messaging/outbox-pattern.
articles.boundary: Agent-specific checkpointing, resumption and human-in-the-loop pauses; general durable execution lives in long-running-operations-async-request-reply-durable-execution.

articles.title: Voice agents: cascaded pipelines vs speech-to-speech models
articles.scope: Compares speech-to-text, text model and text-to-speech cascades with native speech-to-speech models on latency, control, voice choice and cost. Maps Foundry voice-based prompt agents on Voice Live, hosted-agent Invocations over WebSocket, Amazon Nova Sonic, AgentCore Runtime bidirectional streaming, Strands BidiAgent and the Copilot Studio Customer Conversation harness. Covers telephony channels and handoff to humans.

articles.title: Computer use vs browser automation vs API tools
articles.scope: Contrasts screenshot-driven GUI control, scripted cloud browsers and plain API tools on reliability, security, auditability and cost. Covers Copilot Studio computer use, Foundry computer use (direct integration) and browser automation (Toolbox), AgentCore Browser and Amazon Nova Act. Gives a rule: use an API when one exists.

articles.title: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer
articles.scope: Covers the five canonical building blocks with diagrams, gating checks, aggregation strategies and cost profiles. Maps each to Agent Framework workflows, Azure Logic Apps, Copilot Studio workflows, Bedrock Flows, Step Functions and LangGraph, with a callout that Foundry workflows retire on 2026-12-01. Also covers (merged from llm-workflow-patterns): Catalogs code-defined workflows: chains with validation gates, conditional routing, fan-out and map-reduce, evaluator-optimizer and self-critique loops, and hybrids where a rules engine decides. Contrasts workflows with model-directed agents (ai/agents). Tabs compare Amazon Bedrock Flows (versions, aliases) with Microsoft Agent Framework workflows, noting prompt flow retires 2027-04-20.

articles.title: Single agent vs supervisor vs network vs group chat
articles.scope: Compares one agent with many tools against supervisor, sequential, concurrent, group-chat, magentic and swarm topologies. Weighs context isolation, token multiplication, coordination failure and debuggability, including Copilot Studio guidance to split agents when 30-40 actions degrade tool selection. Explains when splitting helps and when it only adds cost.

articles.title: Handoffs vs agents-as-tools vs A2A delegation
articles.scope: Contrasts transferring control of a conversation, calling another agent and getting its result back, and delegating across an organizational boundary over A2A. Covers context passing, accountability and user experience, with examples in the OpenAI Agents SDK, Agent Framework handoff orchestration, Copilot Studio child and connected agents, Strands and AgentCore Harness.

articles.title: Bounding agent behaviour: budgets, stop conditions and tool limits
articles.scope: Covers the reliability side of agent safety: iteration and token budgets, timeouts, loop detection, circuit breakers, least-privilege tool scopes, sandboxing and egress limits. Maps to Foundry oversight controls and hosted-agent egress rules (preview), AgentCore Policy and IAM resource boundaries. Threat content is linked to security/ai-security, not repeated.

articles.title: Hybrid LLM and deterministic rules: when the model should not decide
articles.scope: Shows how to split work between a probabilistic model and deterministic code: rules engines, schema-enforced outputs, text-to-SQL for exact answers, policy checks before tool execution and formal verification of answers. Maps to Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks, AgentCore Policy (Dogwood, Cedar-compatible), Strands Cedar authorization and Copilot Studio standard-harness topics.

articles.title: Agent evaluation: system vs process (trajectory) evaluation
articles.scope: Covers task completion, intent resolution, task adherence and tool-call accuracy, trajectory matching (exact, in-order, any-order), simulated users, golden datasets, offline vs continuous evaluation, CI quality gates, and business alignment metrics (task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction). Maps to Foundry agent evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations, Copilot Studio test sets and grader library, and Bedrock Agents Classic evaluations. LLM-as-judge mechanics link to ai/evaluation-ops.

articles.title: Tracing and monitoring agents with OpenTelemetry
articles.scope: Covers spans for model calls, tool calls and handoffs, the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions vs OpenInference, MCP trace-context propagation in _meta, token and latency breakdowns, safety signals and multi-agent coordination tracking. Implements the same instrumentation in Foundry with Application Insights and AgentCore Observability with CloudWatch generative AI observability, plus Copilot Studio analytics and user-feedback analysis.

articles.title: Agent identity and authorization: delegated vs autonomous access
articles.scope: Treats agents as non-human workload identities. Contrasts on-behalf-of and token-exchange delegation with autonomous app-only access, and covers scoped capabilities, per-tool consent, audience-bound tokens and confused-deputy risk. Maps to Entra Agent ID, Foundry agent identities, AgentCore Identity and MCP authorization. Links security/iam workload-identity and capability-based-authz pages at their new paths.

articles.title: Governing an agent fleet: registry, policy, audit and decommissioning
articles.scope: Covers inventory and registries, immutable versions and promotion, policy enforcement, audit trails and retirement. Compares Foundry Control Plane (including registered agents from other platforms), Microsoft Agent 365 and Entra Agent Registry, Copilot Studio agent inventory, AgentCore Registry (publish, review, approve) and Policy. Frameworks link to security/grc and security/ai-security.

articles.title: Agent ALM and CI/CD: versions, environments, evaluation gates and IaC
articles.scope: Designs ALM for agents, prompts, tools, knowledge data and custom models: environments, immutable versions, promotion, evaluation gates, rollback and audit. Implements Foundry hosted agents with azd and pipelines, AgentCore versions and endpoints with CDK or CloudFormation, and Foundry projects with Bicep and Terraform; links Copilot Studio and Dynamics 365 ALM pages.

articles.title: Agent cost model, ROI and TCO
articles.scope: Explains token multiplication in loops and multi-agent systems, per-session compute (Foundry hosted agents bill CPU and memory per active session; AgentCore Runtime bills active processing, typically not I/O waits), tool and agentic-retrieval token billing, caching and Copilot Credits. Builds an ROI and TCO worksheet with cost per interaction. Links architecture/cost.

articles.title: The agent optimization loop: traces, evaluations, recommendations, A/B tests
articles.scope: Describes the improve loop: collect traces, score them, generate changes to instructions, tool descriptions, skills or model choice, then validate with controlled experiments. Compares Foundry agent optimizer (preview) with AgentCore Optimization (recommendations, configuration bundles, A/B tests via Gateway traffic splitting).

articles.title: Where agent code runs: code interpreters, sandboxes and egress control
articles.scope: Compares the Foundry code interpreter and per-session VM sandboxes with egress controls (preview), AgentCore Code Interpreter, Runtime microVMs and Harness shell, Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions and OpenSandbox. Covers resource boundaries, network egress and secrets. Links security/appsec Wasm sandboxing.

articles.title: Agent failure modes and troubleshooting
articles.scope: A catalog of symptoms, causes, trace signals and fixes: infinite loops, wrong tool or arguments, hallucinated tools, context overflow and truncation, early termination, goal drift, stale memory and cascading multi-agent failures. Supports the troubleshooting and error-analysis objectives.

articles.title: Agent frameworks compared
articles.scope: A matrix of Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK (Foundry docs: Anthropic Agent SDK), GitHub Copilot SDK, Strands Agents, Google ADK and Agent Squad. Dimensions: abstractions, languages and .NET availability, state and durability, multi-agent primitives, MCP and A2A support, observability, and hosting on Foundry hosted agents or AgentCore Runtime.

articles.title: Microsoft Agent Framework (successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen)
articles.scope: Covers agents, the Harness Agent (planning, compaction, file access, memory, tool approval), sessions, context providers, middleware, MCP clients and FoundryToolbox, and workflows with executors, edges, checkpoints, human-in-the-loop and declarative YAML. Includes the built-in orchestrations and a migration map from Semantic Kernel, AutoGen and Foundry workflows. C# and Python side by side; Go is preview.

articles.title: LangGraph in depth: state graphs, checkpointers and interrupts
articles.scope: Covers state graphs, nodes and edges, checkpointers, interrupts for human input, durable execution and LangSmith Deployment. Uses LangGraph as the cross-cloud reference framework, deployed to Foundry hosted agents and AgentCore Runtime and evaluated with AgentCore Evaluations.

articles.title: Strands Agents: the model-driven AWS SDK
articles.scope: Covers the model-driven loop, tools and MCP, model providers, hooks, session persistence, interventions with Cedar authorization, BidiAgent voice streaming and multi-agent patterns (agents as tools, swarm, graph, workflow, A2A). Ends with deployment to AgentCore Runtime, Lambda, Fargate or EKS. Python and TypeScript only; C# readers use the AWS SDK for .NET.

articles.title: Harness SDKs compared: Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, GitHub Copilot SDK, Agent Framework Harness Agent
articles.scope: Compares batteries-included agent SDKs on loop design, permissions, sandboxing, sessions, MCP, skills and hooks. States languages per SDK (the GitHub Copilot SDK and Agent Framework have .NET; the Claude and OpenAI SDKs are Python and TypeScript). Shows which can run as Foundry hosted agents or AgentCore code-defined agents.

articles.title: What is MCP? Hosts, clients, servers and why a protocol
articles.scope: Foundation introduction: the M×N integration problem, host, client and server roles, tools, resources and prompts, and local vs remote servers. Compares MCP with plain function calling. Afterwards the reader can explain MCP's role in connecting agents to external systems.

articles.title: MCP vs custom function-calling and OpenAPI tools
articles.scope: Expands the existing stub, moved from messaging/. Covers when to expose capabilities as an MCP server vs in-process function tools vs OpenAPI tools, trust boundaries of local stdio vs remote Streamable HTTP, sandboxed tool runners, gateways, and per-request auth with server-minted handles passed as tool arguments. Fixes the stale scope: HTTP+SSE has been deprecated since 2025-03-26 (2026-07-28 only reclassifies it), and protocol sessions no longer exist.

articles.title: MCP architecture and primitives in depth
articles.scope: Covers tools (model-controlled), resources (application-controlled) and prompts (user-controlled), per-request _meta, server/discover, elicitation through Multi Round-Trip Requests, cacheable list results, and the deprecated roots, sampling and logging features. Builds a server in C# and Python.

articles.title: stdio vs Streamable HTTP
articles.scope: Covers framing, POST-per-message with JSON or request-scoped SSE replies, required MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, x-mcp-header parameters, cancellation by closing the stream, subscriptions/listen and Origin validation against DNS rebinding. Covers hosting stateless servers on Lambda, Azure Functions, Container Apps, ECS and AgentCore Runtime.

articles.title: MCP authorization: OAuth 2.1 for tools
articles.scope: Covers the server as resource server, Protected Resource Metadata discovery, client registration priority (pre-registration, then Client ID Metadata Documents, then deprecated DCR with application_type, then asking the user), credentials keyed by issuer, PKCE, resource indicators, iss validation (RFC 9207), the ban on token passthrough and step-up scopes. Covers the client-credentials and enterprise-managed authorization extensions. OAuth fundamentals link to security/iam.

articles.title: MCP extensions: Apps, Tasks, Skills over MCP and auth extensions
articles.scope: Explains extension identifiers, negotiation through the extensions capability and graceful degradation. Covers MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui), Tasks (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks), Skills over MCP and the two authorization extensions, plus the experimental-extension path.

articles.title: MCP 2026-07-28: from handshake sessions to stateless requests
articles.scope: Compares 2025 revisions with 2026-07-28: no initialize or Mcp-Session-Id, per-request _meta, server/discover, subscriptions/listen, MRTR and resultType, no SSE resumability, Tasks moved to an extension, ttlMs and cacheScope, removed ping, logging/setLevel and roots list_changed, removed elicitation/complete, renumbered error codes, JSON Schema 2020-12, deprecations and the 12-month lifecycle policy. Ends with the backward-compatibility detection matrix.

articles.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1.0
articles.scope: Covers Agent Cards at /.well-known/agent-card.json, skills, supportedInterfaces and tenants, task states, messages, parts, artifacts and contextId, streaming and push notifications, JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON bindings, security schemes, signed and extended cards, and AAIF stewardship. Exposes an agent over A2A from Agent Framework (Foundry A2A v1.0 GA) and Strands (AgentCore Runtime).

articles.title: MCP vs A2A vs AG-UI: tools, agents and users
articles.scope: Positions the three protocols by layer and explains when to wrap an agent as an MCP tool vs publish it over A2A. Places platform protocols: Responses API vs Open Responses, Foundry Invocations and Activity, AgentCore WebSocket streaming and AG-UI hosting. Links frontend/real-time-ui-streaming and messaging/signalr-websockets.

articles.title: AGENTS.md vs Agent Skills vs MCP prompts
articles.scope: Contrasts always-loaded repository instructions (nearest AGENTS.md wins) with on-demand skills (SKILL.md, progressive disclosure), MCP prompts and tool definitions. Covers authoring, scoping and security review of bundled scripts, and support in GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Foundry Toolbox skills, Copilot Studio skills, AgentCore Registry and Skills over MCP.

articles.title: Registries for agents, MCP servers and skills
articles.scope: Covers the official MCP Registry (preview; server.json, DNS or GitHub namespace verification, public servers only, consumed by aggregators rather than hosts) vs private registries, A2A card discovery, Entra Agent Registry and Agent 365, AgentCore Registry and Foundry Control Plane. Treats registries as a supply-chain control point; links security/supply-chain.

articles.title: Cross-cloud agents over A2A and MCP: Foundry to AgentCore
articles.scope: Worked example: a Foundry hosted agent delegates to an AgentCore Runtime agent over A2A, both share tools through Toolbox and Gateway MCP endpoints, and Entra ID is the IdP for the AgentCore inbound JWT authorizer. Contrasts token exchange with forbidden token passthrough and handles MCP revision mismatches.

articles.title: Agent payments: x402 and the Machine Payments Protocol
articles.scope: Explains how agents pay for APIs, MCP servers and content with HTTP 402-style flows, wallets and spending limits, and the fraud and authorization risks. Uses AgentCore Payments as the worked platform. No exam covers it yet.

articles.title: MCP 2026-07-28 cheat sheet
articles.scope: One page: methods, _meta keys, headers, resultType values, error-code ranges and codes (-32020, -32021, -32022, -32602), auth discovery endpoints and status codes, extension identifiers, deprecated features with migrations and lifecycle windows.

articles.title: Anatomy of a managed agent platform
articles.scope: Breaks a platform into model access and gateway, runtime, harness, tool gateway, knowledge and memory, identity, guardrails, evaluation, observability, optimization and registry. Maps each component to Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Bedrock AgentCore with fidelity ratings and links cloud/compare deep dives.

articles.title: The AI gateway pattern
articles.scope: Covers a central proxy for models, tools and agents: auth, token rate limits, quotas and chargeback, semantic and prompt caching, routing and failover, logging and safety. Maps to the API Management AI gateway that Foundry Control Plane uses, AgentCore Gateway model routing, and AAIF Agent Router and agentgateway; provider configuration links to cloud folders. Also covers (merged from genai-gateway-pattern): Designs a layer that enforces auth, per-consumer token quotas, load balancing across deployments and Regions, failover, spillover, degradation, caching, logging and cost attribution so providers switch without code changes. Covers header-driven tier and spillover (x-ms-service-tier, x-ms-spillover-deployment) and Bedrock inference profiles; APIM and API Gateway depth live in cloud folders.

articles.title: Model routing, cascading and fallback for cost and resilience
articles.scope: Moved here from ai/agents/patterns. Covers static, classifier and learned routing, cheap-first cascades, provider switching without code changes (AppConfig, API Gateway, Lambda) and failover with circuit breakers and cross-Region inference. Compares Foundry model router, Bedrock intelligent prompt routing and AgentCore Gateway routing. Also covers (merged from model-routing-and-fallback): Covers static, rule, classifier and learned routing, cascades, ensembles and cross-model or cross-Region fallback behind a gateway. Compares the Foundry model router (Balanced, Quality, Cost; subsets doubling as failover set; smallest-model context; text-only decisions) with Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing (two same-family models, fallback model, quality-difference threshold, English-optimized).

articles.title: Data residency and processing location for AI platforms
articles.scope: Compares Foundry Global, Data Zone and Regional deployments; Bedrock in-Region vs Geo vs Global cross-Region inference and its effect on guardrails and caching; Copilot Studio and Microsoft 365 data movement; third-party tool flows from hosted agents; and Outposts or Wavelength options. Afterwards the reader can validate residency and movement compliance.

articles.title: Choosing an agent platform: prebuilt, extend, low-code or pro-code
articles.scope: A build-buy-extend framework comparing prebuilt agents, Microsoft 365 declarative agents, Copilot Studio, Foundry prompt and hosted agents, AgentCore Harness and Runtime, and Amazon Quick on capability, control, skills, cost and governance. Includes ROI criteria and prebuilt-agent use cases.

articles.title: Case study: a customer-service agent estate on Azure and AWS
articles.scope: Designs the same service on both clouds: Copilot Studio Customer Conversation harness, Foundry hosted agents and Dynamics 365 Contact Center vs Amazon Connect with AgentCore Harness and Runtime. Covers escalation to humans, voice, identity, evaluation, cost and governance, with the trade-offs recorded.

articles.title: Microsoft Foundry: resources, projects and the platform map
articles.scope: Covers the Foundry resource and projects vs legacy hubs, the new and classic portals, Foundry Models, Tools, Agent Service, IQ and Control Plane, SDKs, azd and the Microsoft Foundry Skill. Includes the renamed RBAC roles and a table of what each former service and API became (Assistants to Responses, threads to conversations), with Bicep, Terraform and SDK setup. Also covers (merged from azure-ai-services-orientation): Maps Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry), Foundry Models including Azure OpenAI, Foundry Agent Service, Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services) for vision, language, speech and content extraction, Azure AI Search and Azure Machine Learning, and how they use this section's services (dynamic sessions, Functions, APIM AI gateway, data stores, Key Vault, Monitor, Defender for AI). Orientation only; links ai/platforms and security/ai-security. Also covers (merged from foundry-tools-prebuilt-ai-services): Renamed from foundry-tools-catalog. Orients on Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services): Speech and Voice Live, Language (including CLU), Translator, Vision, Custom Vision, Content Understanding, Document Intelligence, Content Safety and Azure AI Search, and lists retired or retiring services (LUIS, QnA Maker, Personalizer, Content Moderator, Anomaly Detector, Metrics Advisor). Gives specialized-service vs multimodal-model rules and AWS counterparts; workload depth lives in ai/applied.

articles.title: Your first Foundry chat client and prompt agent in Python and C#
articles.scope: Deploys a model and uses the playground, builds a lightweight chat client with the Foundry SDK and an OpenAI client on the project endpoint with keyless auth, then creates a prompt agent in the portal and calls it from a small client. Python first (exam language), C# alongside.

articles.title: Foundry Models and Azure OpenAI: deployment types, quotas and routing
articles.scope: Covers models sold by Azure vs from partners, deployment types (Global, Data Zone, Regional Standard, Provisioned, Batch, Developer), TPM quotas and spillover, v1 routes and the Responses API, keyless Entra auth and the model router. Gives decision rules for an LLM, an SLM, a multimodal model or a Foundry Tool.

articles.title: Fine-tuning and custom models in Foundry: when, which method, how to govern
articles.scope: Decides when to customize vs prompt or ground, and when an SLM fits. Covers SFT, DPO, RFT and distillation, training tiers, Developer deployments for evaluation, validation criteria and eval gates, lineage, required roles, and access control on tuning data.

articles.title: Foundry Agent Service: prompt, voice-based and hosted agents
articles.scope: Covers the three agent types and ephemeral agents on the Responses API, conversations, versions, tools and memory, publishing to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and the Entra Agent Registry, and protocols (Responses, OpenResponses and Activity for Microsoft 365, Invocations, A2A 1.0 GA and 0.3 preview). Covers private networking for prompt agents and BYO Cosmos DB, Storage and AI Search; builds a prompt agent in C# and Python.

articles.title: Deploy a hosted agent on Foundry
articles.scope: Packages an Agent Framework, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Anthropic Agent SDK or GitHub Copilot SDK agent as a container or zip and deploys with azd and CI/CD. Configures protocols, sandbox size, idle timeout (2-240 minutes), $HOME and /files, the state store, background and resilient modes, agent identity and OBO, BYO VNet, egress rules (preview) and private ACR (projects after 2026-06-25). Versions are immutable with no traffic splitting; billing is CPU and memory per active session.

articles.title: Multi-agent orchestration on Foundry after workflows retire
articles.scope: Foundry workflows (preview) retire on 2026-12-01. Shows the three documented paths: export the YAML and run Agent Framework declarative or code workflows as hosted agents, use Azure Logic Apps to call Foundry agents, or connect agents over A2A. Builds sequential, group-chat and human-in-the-loop flows.

articles.title: Foundry tools and the Toolbox MCP endpoint
articles.scope: A matrix of tools by Toolbox vs direct integration: MCP, web search, Azure AI Search, code interpreter, file search, OpenAPI, A2A, browser automation, Fabric IQ and Work IQ in both; tool search and skills Toolbox-only; computer use, SharePoint, Azure Functions, function calling, image generation and memory as direct integrations. Covers immutable versions and default promotion, consumer vs developer endpoints, require_approval, guardrails and auth options.

articles.title: Azure AI Search and Foundry IQ for grounding agents
articles.scope: Covers indexes, vector, hybrid and semantic ranking, skillsets, agentic retrieval with knowledge bases and indexed or remote knowledge sources, retrieval reasoning effort, the MCP retrieval endpoint, file search vs Foundry IQ, token billing and index health. Notes that the GA API (2026-04-01) is minimal and extractive while query planning and answer synthesis are preview (2026-08-01-preview). RAG design links to ai/applied.

articles.title: Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety
articles.scope: Covers guardrails, controls and risks with an applicability matrix: intervention points (tool call and tool response are agent-only preview), actions (agents support only annotate-and-block), model-only risks (spotlighting, groundedness), Microsoft.DefaultV2 and agent override of the model guardrail. Notes guardrails apply only to Foundry Agent Service agents, plus hosted-agent egress controls. Attack theory links to security/ai-security.

articles.title: Foundry evaluation, tracing and the agent optimizer
articles.scope: Covers built-in agent, RAG and safety evaluators, composite evaluators, the AI Red Teaming Agent, tracing to Application Insights, continuous evaluation, dashboards and the agent optimizer (preview), including voice-agent evaluation limits.

articles.title: Foundry Control Plane: fleet inventory, compliance and the AI gateway
articles.scope: Covers fleet inventory of Foundry and registered external agents, models and tools, compliance policies with Azure Policy, Defender and Purview, the API Management AI gateway needed for advanced governance, quota and cost. Explains which controls apply to external agents and which apply only to Foundry Agent Service agents.

articles.title: Securing Foundry: keyless auth, agent identities, RBAC and private networking
articles.scope: Configures Entra keyless auth (keys bypass RBAC), project managed identity vs per-agent identity, renamed Foundry roles and agent-scope assignments, network-secured prompt agents, BYO VNet and egress for hosted agents, private ACR, BYO resources, CMK and Key Vault connections. Links cloud/azure for Private Link, Key Vault and Entra.

articles.title: Copilot Studio agents, workflows and harnesses
articles.scope: Covers agents vs workflows vs agent flows, and the GitHub Copilot, Customer Conversation and standard harnesses (reasoning, multi-agent customer service with human escalation, and topic-based NLU). Covers knowledge, connectors, MCP, computer use, prompt actions, skills, memory, voice and reasoning behaviours, child vs connected agents and external agents (A2A, Foundry, Fabric, Microsoft 365 Agents SDK).

articles.title: Topics vs NLU vs CLU vs generative orchestration in Copilot Studio
articles.scope: Answers when to use standard NLU topics (with fallback), custom CLU in Azure Language (LUIS is retired) or generative orchestration, and maps that exam vocabulary to today's standard vs GitHub Copilot harness. AWS counterpart: Amazon Lex (partial).

articles.title: Extending Microsoft 365 Copilot: declarative vs custom engine agents
articles.scope: Decides when to extend Microsoft 365 Copilot vs build a custom agent. Covers Agent Builder, declarative agents, custom engine agents with the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK and Toolkit, Copilot connectors, actions, MCP, Teams and SharePoint agents, proactive and group scenarios, and cost.

articles.title: Copilot Studio ALM, environments, governance, analytics and evaluations
articles.scope: Designs environment strategy, solutions and pipelines, connection references and environment variables, DLP for connectors and MCP, agent inventory, analytics and user-feedback review, test sets with the shared grader library, test cases generated with Copilot, and Copilot Credits budgeting.

articles.title: Copilot and agents in Dynamics 365
articles.scope: Covers business terms and customizations of Copilot in customer experience and service apps, connectors for Copilot in Dynamics 365 Sales, Contact Center channel integration, AI in finance and supply chain, finance and operations agent chat knowledge sources, in-app help knowledge, Microsoft 365 Copilot for Sales and Service, ALM and end-to-end testing across apps. articles.title: Amazon Bedrock: models, APIs and inference options
articles.scope: Covers the model catalog (including Amazon Nova and Titan), bedrock-runtime vs bedrock-mantle endpoints, Converse, InvokeModel, OpenAI-compatible Responses and Chat Completions, API keys vs SigV4, on-demand, batch, Provisioned Throughput, Geo and Global cross-Region inference, implicit vs explicit prompt caching and per-request metadata tagging. Includes CDK, CloudFormation and Terraform. Also covers (merged from aws-ai-services-orientation): Orients the reader on what each AWS AI offering is for: Bedrock, the AgentCore components, SageMaker AI, Amazon Quick, Q Developer, Kiro, and application services such as Rekognition, Textract, Comprehend, Polly and Transcribe. Maps each to Microsoft Foundry, Azure AI Search and the Copilot offerings. Includes an AIF-C01 service map showing where the library covers each domain's services (depth in ai/platforms, guardrails and governance in security/ai-security). Keeps only the operations angle here: CloudWatch monitoring of Bedrock workloads, GuardDuty AI Protection, KMS and CloudTrail for AI data, AI cost tracking, and the overlap between Lambda MicroVMs and AgentCore Code Interpreter sessions; S3 Vectors is owned by storage-data. Afterwards the reader knows where every AWS AI topic lives in the library. Also covers (merged from aws-ai-services-catalog): Mirrors the Foundry Tools page: Transcribe, Translate, Comprehend, Lex, Polly, Textract, Rekognition, Kendra, Personalize, Augmented AI and Bedrock Data Automation, with specialized-service vs FM rules and Foundry Tools counterparts rated by fidelity.

articles.title: Hosting MCP Servers on Azure and AWS: Functions, API Management, Logic Apps and Container Apps vs Lambda, ECS and AgentCore
articles.scope: Wave 3. Decision factors are transport (streamable HTTP, stateless vs session-bound), auth (OAuth protected-resource metadata with Entra ID or Cognito), scaling and cold start, and cost. Azure options: the Functions MCP extension (GA, with tool and resource triggers), self-hosted MCP SDK servers on Functions (preview, stateless streamable HTTP only), API Management exposing a REST API as an MCP server or proxying an existing one under policies, Logic Apps Standard as an MCP server with connectors as tools, and Container Apps. AWS options: stateless MCP on Lambda, complex long-lived servers on ECS/Fargate, AgentCore Gateway turning OpenAPI, Lambda or Smithy targets into MCP tools with semantic tool search, and AgentCore Runtime hosting MCP servers in isolated sessions. Code uses the C# ModelContextProtocol.AspNetCore and Python mcp/FastMCP SDKs. It links to mcp-transports, mcp-authorization and cross-cloud-agent-interop.

articles.title: Model Deployment Types and Capacity: Foundry Global, Data Zone, Regional, PTU and Batch vs Bedrock On-Demand, Inference Profiles, Service Tiers and Provisioned Throughput
articles.scope: Wave 3. Foundry: deployment types (Global Standard, Data Zone Standard, regional Standard, Global, Data Zone and Regional Provisioned, Global and Data Zone Batch, Developer for fine-tuned models) and where each processes data. Foundry quotas: TPM and RPM per subscription, Region and model, and quota tiers. PTUs: reservations vs hourly, spillover to standard, and 429 and retry-after handling. Bedrock: on-demand, geographic and global cross-Region inference profiles, service tiers (Reserved, Priority, Standard, Flex), Provisioned Throughput model units (needed for most custom models), batch inference, and Service Quotas. SageMaker AI endpoints are the self-hosted option. The article ends with a worked capacity-planning calculation in Python and C# and resilience patterns for service disruption (AIP-C01 1.2.3). It links to ai-data-residency, ai-gateway-pattern and model-routing-and-cascading.

articles.title: Agent Developer Tooling: Foundry Toolkit, azd, Dev Containers and Local Tracing vs AgentCore Starter Toolkit and the Strands Local Loop
articles.scope: Wave 3. Microsoft side: the Foundry Toolkit for VS Code (the new name for AI Toolkit, now also absorbing the separate Foundry extension) with its model playground, agent builder, evaluations and local OpenTelemetry tracing, azd templates and the azd AI agent extension, dev containers, Foundry Local for offline models, and Microsoft Agent Framework DevUI. AWS side: the AgentCore starter toolkit and AgentCore CLI (configure, launch, invoke), the Strands local loop against Bedrock or a local model, and the Aspire dashboard or Jaeger as a local trace viewer. The article shows the inner loop vs the outer loop and how tooling feeds CI/CD (AI-103 1.2.4). It links to microsoft-agent-framework, strands-agents and devops/ai-coding-agents-compared.

terms.definition: A JSON document, usually at /.well-known/agent-card.json, describing an A2A agent's identity, skills, supported interfaces, capabilities and security schemes.
One A2A turn with role user or agent, made of parts (text, file or structured data) and linked to a task and context.

An open protocol at version 1.0, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation, through which agents discover each other via Agent Cards and exchange messages and long-running tasks over JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON.
An Agent Card carrying a signature over its canonical form so clients can verify who published it.
The stateful unit of A2A work, moving through submitted, working, input-required, auth-required and terminal states (completed, failed, canceled, rejected) and returning artifacts.
The Microsoft 365 and Bot Framework message schema used by Teams and Microsoft 365 channels, which Foundry bridges automatically from the Responses protocol when you publish.
terms.equivalent: aws: none

terms.definition: An open, transport-agnostic event protocol (commonly SSE, also WebSockets or webhooks) for streaming agent runs, messages, tool calls and state to front ends; hosted natively on AgentCore Runtime and via raw SSE on Foundry Invocations.
A management layer for fleet-wide inventory, policy, monitoring and cost oversight of agents built on different platforms.
Systematic measurement of an agent's outcomes and process (task success, tool use, instruction adherence, safety, efficiency) on test sets and in production.
Transferring control of a conversation or task to another agent, which then responds directly instead of returning to the caller.

A pre-built engine that runs the agent loop (tool execution, context management, memory, permissions) so you configure an agent instead of coding the loop; some vendors also use the word for a runtime (Copilot Studio) or an opinionated agent class (Agent Framework).
A distinct, auditable non-human identity for an agent so it can authenticate, receive least-privilege access and have its actions attributed separately from users and apps.
The repeated cycle in which an agent sends context to a model, runs any requested tool calls, appends the results and repeats until a stop condition is met.
Improving an agent's instructions, tool descriptions, skills or model choice from traces and evaluations, validated by controlled experiments such as A/B tests.
A catalog of agents, and often their tools and MCP servers, recording owners, versions and approval state for discovery and governance.
A hosting environment that runs agent code with session isolation, scaling, identity and lifecycle management, whatever framework built the agent.
An isolated execution environment, such as a microVM or per-session VM, where agent-generated code and tools run with restricted filesystem, network and credential access.

An open format, originated by Anthropic and now an Agentic AI Foundation project, that packages procedural know-how as a folder with a SKILL.md file plus optional scripts and resources loaded on demand.
An open-source Python and TypeScript framework, started at AWS Labs, that routes each request to a specialized agent with an intent classifier and offers a SupervisorAgent for agent teams.
A callable capability, such as a function, API, retrieval, code execution or another agent, described to the model by name, description and input schema so the model can request it.
Recording each step of an agent run (model calls, tool calls, handoffs, tokens, latency) as linked spans for debugging and audit.
A managed, isolated cloud browser that agents drive, for example with Playwright, to navigate sites, fill forms and extract information.

pairs.difference: In a workflow the developer's code decides the next step; in an agent the model decides, trading predictability and cost control for flexibility.
A prompt-and-response agent only answers from grounded knowledge; a task agent also acts on other systems, so it needs tool permissions, approvals and audit.
A harness is a finished loop you configure; a framework is a set of building blocks you assemble into your own loop or graph.
A harness decides how the agent thinks and acts; a runtime decides where and how securely the code runs. Copilot Studio uses 'harness' for both.
ReAct re-decides after every observation (adaptive, long token trail); plan-and-execute commits to a plan first (cheaper, easier to audit) but must detect when to re-plan.
Reflection is usually one model critiquing itself; evaluator-optimizer separates generator and evaluator roles, often with different models and explicit criteria, in a bounded loop.
Short-term memory is the session's raw context and is compacted or lost; long-term memory is extracted and retrieved across sessions, raising privacy and staleness issues.
Memory is learned from interactions and scoped to users; a knowledge base is curated content indexed ahead of time, with different owners, update paths and access controls.
Compaction summarizes old context, keeping its gist at the cost of a model call; pruning drops it outright, which is cheaper but loses detail.

Prompt caching still calls the model but reuses a processed identical prefix; semantic caching skips the model call by returning a stored answer for a similar request, which risks stale or wrong answers.
In-the-loop blocks until a human approves each gated action; on-the-loop lets the agent proceed while humans monitor and can stop it.
Durable execution preserves which steps finished so a process can resume; memory preserves information for future reasoning. Neither replaces the other.
Function calling is a model API capability for tools declared in-process by one app; MCP is a wire protocol that lets any compliant host discover and call tools on independent servers.
A handoff transfers control so the new agent talks to the user; agent-as-tool keeps the caller in charge and returns only the result.
Splitting isolates context and specializes instructions but multiplies tokens and adds coordination failures; prefer one agent until tool count or context size measurably hurts accuracy.
Sectioning splits work by a scheme fixed in code; in orchestrator-workers a model decides at run time how many subtasks there are.
The routing pattern sends an input to a specialized prompt, tool or agent by topic; a model router picks which model serves the same request by difficulty and cost.
An AI gateway governs model traffic (quotas, routing, caching); an MCP gateway aggregates tools behind one MCP endpoint. Products such as AgentCore Gateway now do both.
Final-response evaluation misses lucky or unsafe paths; trajectory evaluation checks tool calls, arguments and order even when the answer is right.
Tracing records what happened; evaluation judges whether it was good. Evaluations are often computed from traces but answer a different question.
Delegated access is bounded by both the user's rights and the agent's scopes; autonomous access uses the agent's own permissions and needs separate least-privilege design and audit.
MCP connects an agent to tools and data it controls; A2A connects independent agents as peers that negotiate long-running tasks and keep their internals opaque.
A2A delegates tasks between agents; AG-UI streams an agent's events, state and tool activity to a human-facing front end.
MCP Apps lets a tool server ship UI that the host renders inline; AG-UI is the agent-to-front-end event stream the application itself renders.
The model decides to invoke a tool, which may have side effects; resources are read-only context the application or user chooses to include.
stdio runs a local subprocess that trusts the launching user and reads credentials from the environment; Streamable HTTP is a network endpoint needing OAuth, Origin validation and stateless scaling.

2025 revisions opened a stateful session with initialize and Mcp-Session-Id; 2026-07-28 makes every request self-contained with _meta, uses server/discover and replaces server-initiated requests with MRTR.
An MCP task is a durable handle for one long tool operation that the client polls; an A2A task is a multi-turn unit of delegated work between agents with its own states, messages and artifacts.
Sampling, now deprecated, asked the host's model for a completion; elicitation asks the human for input and remains supported through MRTR.
Passthrough forwards a token issued for one audience to another service, which MCP forbids; exchange obtains a new audience-bound token for the downstream API.
AGENTS.md is always-loaded repository guidance; skills are on-demand procedures loaded through progressive disclosure, so they scale without bloating context.
A skill teaches the agent how to do a task, with instructions and scripts it runs itself; a tool is a capability it calls on a server whose internals it cannot see.
The Responses API is OpenAI's product API that Foundry and Bedrock also serve; Open Responses is an AAIF project defining a provider-neutral format modelled on it.
Semantic Kernel centred on kernels and plugins; Agent Framework is its successor, merging AutoGen-style multi-agent abstractions with graph workflows, checkpoints and a Harness Agent.
Agent Framework offers explicit typed workflow graphs and first-class .NET; Strands is model-driven, Python and TypeScript only, and paired with AgentCore.
Both embed a production coding-agent loop, but the Copilot SDK drives the Copilot CLI over JSON-RPC and ships a .NET SDK, while the Claude Agent SDK is Python and TypeScript only.
A prompt agent is configuration that Foundry runs; a hosted agent is your own code in a per-session sandbox, which you size, version and pay compute for.
File search indexes uploaded files for one agent with no design work; Foundry IQ is a shared, permission-aware knowledge base over many sources built on Azure AI Search agentic retrieval.
Agent flows are the established Power Automate-style format; workflows are the newer designer in which each step can reason and act, with built-in testing and HITL controls.
A child agent lives inside one agent and shares its settings and lifecycle; a connected agent is published separately with its own ALM and channels.
Topics give scripted, predictable paths matched by NLU; generative orchestration lets the model pick knowledge, tools and agents, gaining flexibility but losing determinism.
A declarative agent reuses Microsoft 365 Copilot's orchestrator and models; a custom engine agent brings its own, gaining control at the cost of more effort.

Foundry Control Plane governs AI assets from the Azure side (models, tools, agents, Azure Policy); Agent 365 governs agents as Microsoft 365 workforce members through the admin center, Entra, Purview and Defender.
Agents Classic uses fixed orchestration stages with prompt overrides and is closed to new customers; the Harness is one configurable loop with tools behind Gateway and no stage-specific overrides.
Grounding checks score statistically whether a response matches the source; Automated Reasoning verifies it against formal rules derived from policy documents.
Bedrock is serverless access to hosted foundation models; SageMaker AI is for training, tuning and hosting models on infrastructure you size and pay for.
